claim: Hearing and balance involve the transduction of mechanical stimuli into electrical signals by deflection of bundles of stereocilia linked together by protocadherin 15 (PCDH15) and cadherin 23 'tip links'.
source: Hearing and balance involve the transduction of mechanical stimuli into electrical signals by deflection of bundles of stereocilia linked together by protocadherin 15 (PCDH15) and cadherin 23 'tip links'.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about the mechanism of hearing and balance.

claim: PCDH15 transduces tip link tension into opening of a mechano-electrical transduction (MET) ion channel.
source: PCDH15 transduces tip link tension into opening of a mechano-electrical transduction (MET) ion channel.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about PCDH15 function.

claim: PCDH15 interacts with LHFPL5, a candidate subunit of the MET channel.
source: PCDH15 also interacts with LHFPL5, a candidate subunit of the MET channel.
evidence: This is supported by prior research and the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The PCDH15-LHFPL5 complex is composed of PCDH15 and LHFPL5 subunit pairs related by a 2-fold axis.
source: Here we illuminate the PCDH15-LHFPL5 structure, showing how the complex is composed of PCDH15 and LHFPL5 subunit pairs related by a 2-fold axis.
evidence: This is directly supported by the structural data obtained from cryo-EM studies presented in the manuscript.

claim: The extracellular cadherin domains define a mobile tether coupled to a rigid, 2-fold symmetric 'collar' proximal to the membrane bilayer.
source: The extracellular cadherin domains define a mobile tether coupled to a rigid, 2-fold symmetric 'collar' proximal to the membrane bilayer.
evidence: This is supported by the structural analysis from cryo-EM data presented in the manuscript.

claim: LHFPL5 forms extensive interactions with the PCDH15 transmembrane helices.
source: LHFPL5 forms extensive interactions with the PCDH15 transmembrane helices and stabilizes the overall PCDH15-LHFPL5 assembly.
evidence: This is supported by the structural data from cryo-EM studies presented in the manuscript.

claim: LHFPL5 stabilizes the overall PCDH15-LHFPL5 assembly.
source: LHFPL5 forms extensive interactions with the PCDH15 transmembrane helices and stabilizes the overall PCDH15-LHFPL5 assembly.
evidence: This is inferred from the extensive interactions observed in the structural data.

claim: Hair cells within the cochlea mediate our sensation of sound.
source: In mammals, hair cells within the cochlea mediate our sensation of sound while the detection of movement and our sense of balance originates with hair cells of the utricle and saccule.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the function of hair cells.

claim: The detection of movement and our sense of balance originates with hair cells of the utricle and saccule.
source: In mammals, hair cells within the cochlea mediate our sensation of sound while the detection of movement and our sense of balance originates with hair cells of the utricle and saccule.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the function of hair cells.

claim: Hair cells have a characteristic morphology and harbor actin-filled stereocilia 'staircases'.
source: Hair cells have a characteristic morphology and harbor actin-filled stereocilia 'staircases' in which the stereocilia are coupled by protocadherin 15 (PCDH15) molecules from one stereocilium linked with cadherin 23 (CDH23) molecules from an adjacent stereocilium (Kazmierczak et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Stereocilia are coupled by protocadherin 15 (PCDH15) molecules from one stereocilium linked with cadherin 23 (CDH23) molecules from an adjacent stereocilium.
source: Hair cells have a characteristic morphology and harbor actin-filled stereocilia 'staircases' in which the stereocilia are coupled by protocadherin 15 (PCDH15) molecules from one stereocilium linked with cadherin 23 (CDH23) molecules from an adjacent stereocilium (Kazmierczak et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Upon movement of the stereocilia induced by fluctuations of the surrounding fluid, the PCDH15-CDH23 'tip links' trigger the opening of a mechano-electrical transduction (MET) ion channel at the stereocilia tips.
source: Upon movement of the stereocilia induced by fluctuations of the surrounding fluid, the PCDH15-CDH23 'tip links' trigger the opening of a mechano-electrical transduction (MET) ion channel at the stereocilia tips (Beurg et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The molecular composition of the MET channel is enigmatic.
source: While the molecular composition of the MET channel is enigmatic (Wu and Müller, 2016; Corey and Holt, 2016), the fundamental role of PCDH15 in coupling the movement of the stereocilia to the gating of the MET channel is unambiguous and conserved throughout vertebrates, such as mammals (Jaiganesh et al., 2017), birds (Ahmed et al., 2006) and fish (Maeda et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research indicating the uncertainty about MET channel composition.

claim: The fundamental role of PCDH15 in coupling the movement of the stereocilia to the gating of the MET channel is unambiguous and conserved throughout vertebrates.
source: While the molecular composition of the MET channel is enigmatic (Wu and Müller, 2016; Corey and Holt, 2016), the fundamental role of PCDH15 in coupling the movement of the stereocilia to the gating of the MET channel is unambiguous and conserved throughout vertebrates, such as mammals (Jaiganesh et al., 2017), birds (Ahmed et al., 2006) and fish (Maeda et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research across different vertebrate species.

claim: In vertebrates PCDH15 regulates the development and function of stereocilia in hair cells.
source: Moreover, in vertebrates PCDH15 regulates the development and function of stereocilia in hair cells (Webb et al., 2011) while its homolog in flies is essential for the microvilli morphology in follicle cells (D'Alterio et al., 2005; Schlichting et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The PCDH15 homolog in flies is essential for the microvilli morphology in follicle cells.
source: Moreover, in vertebrates PCDH15 regulates the development and function of stereocilia in hair cells (Webb et al., 2011) while its homolog in flies is essential for the microvilli morphology in follicle cells (D'Alterio et al., 2005; Schlichting et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: In humans, mutations in PCDH15 cause Usher syndrome type 1, an inherited deaf-blindness together with vestibular dysfunction and unintelligible speech.
source: In humans, mutations in PCDH15 cause Usher syndrome type 1, an inherited deaf-blindness together with vestibular dysfunction and unintelligible speech, as well as nonsyndromic recessive hearing loss (DFNB23) (Ahmed et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Mutations in PCDH15 cause nonsyndromic recessive hearing loss (DFNB23).
source: In humans, mutations in PCDH15 cause Usher syndrome type 1, an inherited deaf-blindness together with vestibular dysfunction and unintelligible speech, as well as nonsyndromic recessive hearing loss (DFNB23) (Ahmed et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: PCDH15 belongs to the cadherin superfamily.
source: PCDH15 belongs to the cadherin superfamily and consists of 11 extracellular cadherin (EC) domains, an extracellular linker (EL) domain, a single transmembrane (TM) helix and a cytoplasmic domain.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about PCDH15 classification.

claim: PCDH15 consists of 11 extracellular cadherin (EC) domains, an extracellular linker (EL) domain, a single transmembrane (TM) helix and a cytoplasmic domain.
source: PCDH15 belongs to the cadherin superfamily and consists of 11 extracellular cadherin (EC) domains, an extracellular linker (EL) domain, a single transmembrane (TM) helix and a cytoplasmic domain.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about PCDH15 structure.

claim: Three evolutionarily conserved PCDH15 splice isoforms differ in the C-terminal region of the cytoplasmic domains (CD1, CD2 and CD3).
source: Three evolutionarily conserved PCDH15 splice isoforms differ in the C-terminal region of the cytoplasmic domains (CD1, CD2 and CD3) (Ahmed et al., 2008), but share a common region (CR) following the TM helix (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The three PCDH15 splice isoforms share a common region (CR) following the TM helix.
source: Three evolutionarily conserved PCDH15 splice isoforms differ in the C-terminal region of the cytoplasmic domains (CD1, CD2 and CD3) (Ahmed et al., 2008), but share a common region (CR) following the TM helix (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research and reference to Figure 1a.

claim: The complex of PCDH15 with CDH23 has been characterized by x-ray crystallography, revealing a 'hand-shake' antiparallel interaction of the two most N-terminal cadherin repeats of both proteins.
source: The complex of PCDH15 with CDH23 has been characterized by x-ray crystallography, revealing a 'hand-shake' antiparallel interaction of the two most N-terminal cadherin repeats of both proteins (Sotomayor et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Immunoprecipitation and two-hybrid experiments suggest that PCDH15 interacts with transmembrane channel-like protein 1 and 2 (TMC1, TMC2).
source: Immunoprecipitation and two-hybrid experiments suggest that PCDH15 interacts with several likely MET channel components, including transmembrane channel-like protein 1 and 2 (TMC1, TMC2) (Pan et al., 2013; Maeda et al., 2014; Beurg et al., 2015), lipoma HMGIC fusion partner-like 5 (LHFPL5, also known as TMHS) (Xiong et al., 2012), and transmembrane inner ear protein (TMIE) (Zhao et al., 2014), although none of these studies have isolated stable and biochemically well behaved complexes.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Immunoprecipitation and two-hybrid experiments suggest that PCDH15 interacts with lipoma HMGIC fusion partner-like 5 (LHFPL5, also known as TMHS).
source: Immunoprecipitation and two-hybrid experiments suggest that PCDH15 interacts with several likely MET channel components, including transmembrane channel-like protein 1 and 2 (TMC1, TMC2) (Pan et al., 2013; Maeda et al., 2014; Beurg et al., 2015), lipoma HMGIC fusion partner-like 5 (LHFPL5, also known as TMHS) (Xiong et al., 2012), and transmembrane inner ear protein (TMIE) (Zhao et al., 2014), although none of these studies have isolated stable and biochemically well behaved complexes.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Immunoprecipitation and two-hybrid experiments suggest that PCDH15 interacts with transmembrane inner ear protein (TMIE).
source: Immunoprecipitation and two-hybrid experiments suggest that PCDH15 interacts with several likely MET channel components, including transmembrane channel-like protein 1 and 2 (TMC1, TMC2) (Pan et al., 2013; Maeda et al., 2014; Beurg et al., 2015), lipoma HMGIC fusion partner-like 5 (LHFPL5, also known as TMHS) (Xiong et al., 2012), and transmembrane inner ear protein (TMIE) (Zhao et al., 2014), although none of these studies have isolated stable and biochemically well behaved complexes.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: None of the prior studies have isolated stable and biochemically well behaved complexes of PCDH15 with TMC1, TMC2, LHFPL5, or TMIE.
source: Immunoprecipitation and two-hybrid experiments suggest that PCDH15 interacts with several likely MET channel components, including transmembrane channel-like protein 1 and 2 (TMC1, TMC2) (Pan et al., 2013; Maeda et al., 2014; Beurg et al., 2015), lipoma HMGIC fusion partner-like 5 (LHFPL5, also known as TMHS) (Xiong et al., 2012), and transmembrane inner ear protein (TMIE) (Zhao et al., 2014), although none of these studies have isolated stable and biochemically well behaved complexes.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research and the authors' assessment of those studies.

claim: No structural information is available to illuminate the interactions of PCDH15 and MET channel components.
source: Moreover, no structural information is available to illuminate the interactions of PCDH15 and these MET channel components.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge prior to this study.

claim: The low abundance of hair cells and tip links within these cells limits biochemical and structural studies of the native tip link and its interactions.
source: The low abundance of hair cells and tip links within these cells limits biochemical and structural studies of the native tip link and its interactions (Effertz et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: PCDH15 forms a robust and monodisperse complex with LHFPL5.
source: We thus screened co-expression of PCDH15 with TMC1, LHFPL5, or TMIE in a heterologous mammalian expression system and found that PCDH15 forms a robust and monodisperse complex with LHFPL5.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data from the screening experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: PCDH154EC alone displayed multiple peaks in the chromatogram, indicating that it was polydisperse when expressed in isolation.
source: PCDH154EC alone displayed multiple peaks in the chromatogram, indicating that it was polydisperse when expressed in isolation (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: Coexpression of LHFPL5 resulted in PCDH154EC elution as one major peak.
source: Coexpression of LHFPL5 resulted in PCDH154EC elution as one major peak (Figure 1b), a species that persisted following pulldown of the complex (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b), in accord with previous observations that PCDH15 and LHFPL5 form a complex (Beurg et al., 2015; Xiong et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 1b and Figure 1—figure supplement 1b, and is consistent with prior research.

claim: LHFPL5 eluted with a peak at the same position as the PCDH15 peak, but also showed a large peak at a later elution volume that likely corresponds to free LHFPL5.
source: LHFPL5 eluted with a peak at the same position as the PCDH15 peak, but also showed a large peak at a later elution volume that likely corresponds to free LHFPL5 (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 1c, with inference about the identity of the later peak.

claim: The PCDH15-LHFPL5 complex was isolated by tandem affinity purification, yielding a homogeneous complex that eluted as a single symmetric peak by size exclusion chromatography.
source: We isolated the PCDH15-LHFPL5 complex by tandem affinity purification, yielding a homogeneous complex that eluted as a single symmetric peak by size exclusion chromatography (Figure 1d and e).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 1d and e.

claim: Imaging of the PCDH154EC-LHFPL5 complex by cryo-EM using a Volta phase plate showed particles composed of a micelle-shaped feature with two emerging strands.
source: Imaging of the PCDH154EC-LHFPL5 complex by cryo-EM using a Volta phase plate (Danev and Baumeister, 2016) showed particles composed of a micelle-shaped feature with two emerging strands, where the strands adopt a range of conformations (Figure 2a and Figure 2—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM data shown in Figure 2a and Figure 2—figure supplement 2a.

claim: The strands of the PCDH154EC-LHFPL5 complex adopt a range of conformations.
source: Imaging of the PCDH154EC-LHFPL5 complex by cryo-EM using a Volta phase plate (Danev and Baumeister, 2016) showed particles composed of a micelle-shaped feature with two emerging strands, where the strands adopt a range of conformations (Figure 2a and Figure 2—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM data shown in Figure 2a and Figure 2—figure supplement 2a.

claim: A 3D reconstruction of the straight conformation of the PCDH154EC-LHFPL5 complex was computed at ~11.3 Å resolution.
source: We proceeded to carry out a 3D reconstruction and computed a reconstruction at ~11.3 Å resolution of this straight conformation (Figure 2c, Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2c and d, and Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM data and processing described in the manuscript.

claim: The two density features protruding from the micelle are ~190 Å in length and ~20 Å in diameter, consistent with an approximately linear chain of four cadherin domains.
source: The two density features protruding from the micelle are ~190 Å in length and ~20 Å in diameter, consistent with an approximately linear chain of four cadherin domains.
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM data and structural analysis.

claim: At the base of the protruding density, proximal to the micelle, is a disk-shaped density that appears to be formed by the C-terminal part of EC11 and the ~100 residue EL domain.
source: At the base of the protruding density, proximal to the micelle, is a disk-shaped density that appears to be formed by the C-terminal part of EC11 and the ~100 residue EL domain.
evidence: This is inferred from the cryo-EM density and knowledge of the protein structure.

claim: The micelle shows two protrusions 'underneath' the disk-shaped EC11-EL density.
source: The micelle shows two protrusions 'underneath' the disk-shaped EC11-EL density.
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM density.

claim: LHFPL5 contains four α-helices that cross the membrane, intracellular termini, and an extracellular β-strand rich domain that could account for the protrusions underneath the disk-shaped EC11-EL density.
source: LHFPL5 contains four α-helices that cross the membrane, intracellular termini, and an extracellular β-strand rich domain that could account for these protrusions.
evidence: This is inferred from knowledge of LHFPL5 structure and the cryo-EM density.

claim: On the intracellular side of the micelle density, there are only minor protrusions that might belong to either PCDH15 or LHFPL5, indicating that the cytoplasmic regions of both proteins are not well ordered.
source: On the intracellular side of the micelle density, there are only minor protrusions that might belong to either PCDH15 or LHFPL5, indicating that the cytoplasmic regions of both proteins are not well ordered.
evidence: This is inferred from the cryo-EM density.

claim: A dimer interface is observed between the two cadherin strands formed by the C-terminal half of EC9.
source: We observe a dimer interface between the two cadherin strands formed by the C-terminal half of EC9, largely defined by a loop between β1 and β2 strands and the N-terminus of the α-helix between β3 and β4 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2h).
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2h.

claim: The EC9 dimer interface appears to stabilize the straight conformation.
source: This interface appears to stabilize the straight conformation.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural data.

claim: A second group of particles shows the two cadherin chains bent away from one another, deemed the 'split' conformation.
source: A second group of particles shows the two cadherin chains bent away from one another, deemed the 'split' conformation (Figure 2a, red).
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: In the split conformation, the cadherin chains are parallel for about half of their lengths, from the micelle, before separating.
source: Inspection of 2D class averages indicates that the cadherin chains are parallel for about half of their lengths, from the micelle, before separating (Figure 2b, red and Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by the 2D class averages shown in Figure 2b and Video 1.

claim: The density for the most distal cadherin domains in the split conformation is weak, likely due to conformational flexibility, thus precluding 3D reconstruction.
source: The density for the most distal cadherin domains is weak, likely due to conformational flexibility, thus precluding 3D reconstruction.
evidence: This is inferred from the cryo-EM data.

claim: Fitting EC10 of the EC8-10 crystal structure into the density for EC10 in the reconstruction produces a conformation that has a striking similarity with 2D class averages.
source: Nevertheless, we found that fitting EC10 of the EC8-10 crystal structure into the density for EC10 in our reconstruction produces a conformation that has a striking similarity with 2D class averages (Figure 2—figure supplement 2i).
evidence: This is supported by the comparison shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2i.

claim: In the PCDH154EC construct, the linking polypeptide between EC9 and EC10 can switch between the straight and L conformations.
source: This indicates that in our construct the linking polypeptide between EC9 and EC10 can switch between the straight and L conformations.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural data and comparison with the crystal structure.

claim: The relative populations of the straight and split conformations are approximately equal.
source: We estimate that the relative populations of the straight and split conformations are approximately equal.
evidence: This is estimated from the cryo-EM data.

claim: A third class of particles shows a dramatic bending of the entire extracellular domain relative to the micelle, called the 'tilted' conformation.
source: A third class of particles shows a dramatic bending of the entire extracellular domain relative to the micelle (Figure 2a,b, purple and Video 2). We call this the 'tilted' conformation.
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM data shown in Figure 2a,b and Video 2.

claim: The pronounced conformational mobility in the tilted conformation only occurs in the projection with double-stranded cadherin domains.
source: The pronounced conformational mobility only occurs in the projection with double-stranded cadherin domains (Figure 2c, left), indicating the flexibility is largely within the plane of the cadherin chains.
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: The flexibility in the tilted conformation is largely within the plane of the cadherin chains.
source: The pronounced conformational mobility only occurs in the projection with double-stranded cadherin domains (Figure 2c, left), indicating the flexibility is largely within the plane of the cadherin chains.
evidence: This is inferred from the cryo-EM data.

claim: The two 'linkers' connecting the EL domains to the PCDH15 TM helices act as a 'hinge joint', allowing the entire PCDH15 extracellular domains to swivel about an axis parallel to the axis connecting the two linkers.
source: The two 'linkers' connecting the EL domains to the PCDH15 TM helices act as a 'hinge joint', allowing the entire PCDH15 extracellular domains to swivel about an axis parallel to the axis connecting the two linkers, perhaps facilitating a tilted conformation of the PCDH15 extracellular domains upon formation of the mature tip link.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural data and the observed conformational flexibility.

claim: The hinge joint may facilitate a tilted conformation of the PCDH15 extracellular domains upon formation of the mature tip link.
source: The two 'linkers' connecting the EL domains to the PCDH15 TM helices act as a 'hinge joint', allowing the entire PCDH15 extracellular domains to swivel about an axis parallel to the axis connecting the two linkers, perhaps facilitating a tilted conformation of the PCDH15 extracellular domains upon formation of the mature tip link.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the structural data.

claim: The split and tilted conformations are not two distinct conformations but rather represent views of a large ensemble of conformational states along a continuous range of motion.
source: In all likelihood, the split and tilted conformations are not two distinct conformations but rather represent views of a large ensemble of conformational states along a continuous range of motion.
evidence: This is inferred from the cryo-EM data showing various conformations.

claim: The straight conformation is stabilized by the EC9 dimer interaction and perhaps by favorable interactions with LHFPL5.
source: The observation that the straight population is sampled frequently enough to allow reconstruction of a 3D structure implies that the straight conformation is stabilized by the EC9 dimer interaction and perhaps by favorable interactions with LHFPL5.
evidence: This is inferred from the ability to reconstruct the straight conformation and the observed interactions.

claim: The EC11 domain shows a classic cadherin fold.
source: As expected, the EC11 domain shows a classic cadherin fold (Shapiro et al., 1995), while the EL domain has a ferredoxin-like fold (Adman et al., 1973).
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure and citations to prior research on cadherin folds.

claim: The EL domain has a ferredoxin-like fold.
source: As expected, the EC11 domain shows a classic cadherin fold (Shapiro et al., 1995), while the EL domain has a ferredoxin-like fold (Adman et al., 1973).
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure and a citation to prior research on ferredoxin folds.

claim: Between the second β-strand of the ferredoxin motif (β2) and the third strand (β5) resides a β-hairpin (β3-β4) that, in the context of the complex structure, would likely point toward the membrane.
source: Between the second β-strand of the ferredoxin motif (β2) and the third strand (β5) resides a β-hairpin (β3-β4) that, in the context of the complex structure, would likely point toward the membrane.
evidence: This is inferred from the crystal structure and the context of the complex.

claim: The EC11-EL construct forms a 2-fold symmetric dimer in the crystal lattice.
source: The EC11-EL construct forms a 2-fold symmetric dimer in the crystal lattice (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure shown in Figure 3a.

claim: A direct rigid-body fitting of the EC11-EL dimer, derived from the crystal structure, into the cryo-EM density map of the PCDH154EC-LHFPL5 complex yields a correlation coefficient of 0.94.
source: A direct rigid-body fitting of the EC11-EL dimer, derived from the crystal structure, into the cryo-EM density map of the PCDH154EC-LHFPL5 complex yields a correlation coefficient of 0.94 (Figure 3c).
evidence: This is supported by the fitting analysis shown in Figure 3c.

claim: The EC11-EL dimer has an oval, disk-like shape with long and short axes of 70 Å and 55 Å, respectively.
source: The dimer has an oval, disk-like shape with long and short axes of 70 Å and 55 Å, respectively (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure shown in Figure 3a.

claim: The EC11 and EL domains sit 'side-by-side', providing extensive interactions within each protomer and throughout the dimer interface.
source: Unlike the linear 'top to bottom' arrangement of cadherin domains, the EC11 and EL domains sit 'side-by-side', providing extensive interactions within each protomer and throughout the dimer interface.
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure.

claim: The interactions within each protomer of the EC11-EL dimer are largely mediated by the β2a and β7 strands in EC11, and the β2 and β5 strands in EL, which together form a β-barrel like structure.
source: The interactions within each protomer are largely mediated by the β2a and β7 strands in EC11, and the β2 and β5 strands in EL, which together form a β-barrel like structure.
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure.

claim: A 'major' dimer interface is formed by contacts between EC11 and the EL domain of the symmetry related protomer (EL').
source: A 'major' dimer interface is formed by contacts between EC11 and the EL domain of the symmetry related protomer (EL'). This interface is composed of β4, β5, and β3-β4 loop in EC11, and α1a and β2 in EL' with a buried solvent accessible surface area of ~410 Å2.
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure.

claim: The major dimer interface buries ~410 Å2 of solvent accessible surface area.
source: A 'major' dimer interface is formed by contacts between EC11 and the EL domain of the symmetry related protomer (EL'). This interface is composed of β4, β5, and β3-β4 loop in EC11, and α1a and β2 in EL' with a buried solvent accessible surface area of ~410 Å2.
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure.

claim: A 'minor' dimer interface is defined by contacts between EC11 on one protomer and EC11 on the second protomer (EC11').
source: A 'minor' dimer interface is defined by contacts between EC11 on one protomer and EC11 on the second protomer (EC11'). The minor interface is formed by the guanidino group of Arg1163 and the backbone carbonyl oxygen of Asp1161 (Figure 3a and b) burying 140 Å2 of solvent accessible surface area.
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure shown in Figure 3a and b.

claim: The minor dimer interface buries 140 Å2 of solvent accessible surface area.
source: A 'minor' dimer interface is defined by contacts between EC11 on one protomer and EC11 on the second protomer (EC11'). The minor interface is formed by the guanidino group of Arg1163 and the backbone carbonyl oxygen of Asp1161 (Figure 3a and b) burying 140 Å2 of solvent accessible surface area.
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure.

claim: The C-terminus of the EL domain, which is composed of an α-helix and a loop, extends from the plane of the EC11-EL disk towards the membrane.
source: The C-terminus of the EL domain, which is composed of an α-helix and a loop, extends from the plane of the EC11-EL disk towards the membrane.
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure.

claim: The structure of the C-terminal loop in the soluble EC11-EL construct likely does not represent the conformation in an intact PCDH15 complex.
source: Because the C-terminal loop in the soluble EC11-EL construct is not connected to a TM domain of PCDH15, its structure likely does not represent the conformation in an intact PCDH15 complex.
evidence: This is inferred from the fact that the construct lacks the TM domain.

claim: The EC11-EL structure displays a striking electrostatic potential distribution.
source: The EC11-EL structure displays a striking electrostatic potential distribution (Figure 3—figure supplement 1c–h).
evidence: This is supported by the electrostatic analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1c–h.

claim: EC11, with an isoelectric point (pI) of 9.4, mainly shows a positively charged surface.
source: EC11, with an isoelectric point (pI) of 9.4, mainly shows a positively charged surface, distinct from that of the EC8-10 domains, which have pIs ranging from 4.3 to 4.9.
evidence: This is supported by the electrostatic analysis.

claim: The EC8-10 domains have pIs ranging from 4.3 to 4.9.
source: EC11, with an isoelectric point (pI) of 9.4, mainly shows a positively charged surface, distinct from that of the EC8-10 domains, which have pIs ranging from 4.3 to 4.9.
evidence: This is supported by the electrostatic analysis.

claim: The EL domain has a pI of 5.1 and has a mainly negatively charged surface, except at the C-terminal extended helix, which forms a positive surface together with EC11.
source: The EL domain has a pI of 5.1 and, accordingly, has a mainly negatively charged surface, except at the C-terminal extended helix, which forms a positive surface together with EC11.
evidence: This is supported by the electrostatic analysis.

claim: Residues from α1b and α2b of EL form a negatively charged cavity harboring a deafness mutation, Q1347K.
source: A top-down view of the EC11-EL dimer illustrates how residues from α1b and α2b of EL form a negatively charged cavity harboring a deafness mutation, Q1347K (Ouyang et al., 2005), at the end of the α2b helix.
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure and a citation to prior research on the deafness mutation.

claim: Four conserved arginine residues and one lysine located at the bottom of EC11-EL form a highly positively charged area.
source: We note that four conserved arginine residues and one lysine located at the bottom of EC11-EL form a highly positively charged area (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The function of the basic patch at the bottom of EC11-EL is unknown, but it may participate in interactions with other MET channel components.
source: While the function of this basic patch is unknown, it may participate in interactions with other MET channel components.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the structural data.

claim: There is a strong density in the x-ray maps with a ring-like feature located next to Ser1167, suggestive of O-linked glycosylation.
